metadata.title: Exploring Subjectivity for more Human-Centric Assessment of Social Biases in Large Language Models

abstract: An essential aspect of evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) is identifying potential biases. This is especially relevant considering the substantial evidence that LLMs can replicate human social biases in their text outputs and further influence stakeholders, potentially amplifying harm to already marginalized individuals and communities. Therefore, recent efforts in bias detection invested in automated benchmarks and objective metrics such as accuracy (i.e., an LLMs output is compared against a predefined ground truth). Nonetheless, social biases can be nuanced, oftentimes subjective and context-dependent, where a situation is open to interpretation and there is no ground truth. While these situations can be difficult for automated evaluation systems to identify, human evaluators could potentially pick up on these nuances. In this paper, we discuss the role of human evaluation and subjective interpretation to augment automated processes when identifying biases in LLMs as part of a human-centred approach to evaluate these models.
full_text:
Exploring Subjectivity for more Human-Centric Assessment of
Social Biases in Large Language Models
Paula Akemi Aoyagui
paula.aoyagui@mail.utoronto.ca
University of Toronto
Toronto, Canada
Sharon Ferguson
sharon.ferguson@mail.utoronto.ca
University of Toronto
Toronto, Canada
Anastasia Kuzminykh
anastasia.kuzminykh@utoronto.ca
University of Toronto
Toronto, Canada
ABSTRACT
An essential aspect of evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs)
is identifying potential biases. This is especially relevant consider-
ing the substantial evidence that LLMs can replicate human social
biases in their text outputs and further influence stakeholders, po-
tentially amplifying harm to already marginalized individuals and
communities. Therefore, recent efforts in bias detection invested in
automated benchmarks and objective metrics such as accuracy (i.e.,
an LLMs output is compared against a predefined ground truth).
Nonetheless, social biases can be nuanced, oftentimes subjective
and context-dependent, where a situation is open to interpretation
and there is no ground truth. While these situations can be difficult
for automated evaluation systems to identify, human evaluators
could potentially pick up on these nuances. In this paper, we dis-
cuss the role of human evaluation and subjective interpretation in
augmenting automated processes when identifying biases in LLMs
as part of a human-centred approach to evaluate these models.
CCS CONCEPTS
• Human-centered computing →HCI theory, concepts and
models; HCI design and evaluation methods; Natural lan-
guage interfaces.
KEYWORDS
Human-AI collaboration, Large Language Models, Bias Evaluation,
Human Evaluation, Social Bias, Gender Bias
1
INTRODUCTION
Evaluating biases in Large Language Models (LLMs) is paramount
considering not only their widespread use and popularization but
also the growing concerns that these models can mirror and amplify
harmful biases found in language and society [4, 20, 31, 38, 42]. In
LLMs, social biases manifest, for example, in text outputs that stereo-
type, misrepresent or use derogatory language against a group or
individual based on a characteristic such as race, age, gender, sex-
ual preference, political ideology, religion, etc [11]. For instance,
if a biased LLM powers an automated hiring system designed to
screen hob applicants, there is a risk that some candidates might be
offered better or worse opportunities (i.e. allocational harm) [17].
Similarly, in automated content moderation tasks, an LLM could
miss out on nuances and mistakenly classify text from a specific
group as toxic (i.e., representational harm). Furthermore, beyond
automated system applications, there are potential risks for human-
AI collaboration as well, since past research has pointed humans

might “inherit" biases from an AI system’s recommendations [45].
More specifically, Ferguson et al. [16] demonstrated how an LLM’s
text assessment can affect a human’s text output in both linguistic
characteristics and positionality. Hence, plenty of effort has been
spent developing methods to detect and quantify biases in LLMs.
Bias evaluation in LLMs is most often based on automated meth-
ods and benchmarks [18], with human evaluation mainly used to
verify the results from the automated analysis [11, 14]. Chang et al.
[8]’s survey on LLM evaluation concludes that automated methods
are preferred and more popular mainly because “automatic evalua-
tion does not require intensive human participation, which not only
saves time but also reduces the impact of human subjective factors
and makes the evaluation process more standardized.” However, in
this paper, we argue that subjectivity can play an important role in
bias assessment in LLMs to augment the existing suite of automated
evaluation methods.
2
BACKGROUND
2.1
Bias Evaluation in LLMs
Currently, LLMs are evaluated for social biases using automated
or human evaluation methods. According to Chang et al. [8], the
former leverages metrics that can be “automatically calculated",
while the latter requires human participation. We will briefly discuss
both approaches in this section.
In automated evaluation of biases in LLMs, there are different
processes and metrics available [8, 11, 14, 15, 18, 38]. For example,
Word, sentence or context embedding [7] are based on vector
representations to identify biases in models. However, past work
shows they can be unreliable in detecting biases in text [5, 21].
Similarly, Kaneko et al. [28] consider Token probability (i.e., tech-
niques that measure and compare the likelihood of a model’s pre-
diction under different conditions) can also be insufficient for bias
evaluation and mitigation, especially in downstream tasks. Another
popular bias detection approach involves prompting a model to
then examine the text outputs. These Generated text techniques
include, for instance, Sentiment Analysis of LLM text outputs,
especially popular in the NLP community [30]; however, Sheng
et al. [44] demonstrates that this approach might not be sufficient
to detect more subtle biases in language. Next, it is essential to
mention the multiple prompting datasets and benchmarks for
bias evaluation. For example, adaptations of the Winograd Schema
[32], such as WinoBias [48] and Winogender [40]; the latter offers
datasets with sentences where gender is ambiguous to prompt an
LLM and see which gendered pronoun is chosen; for example: The
paramedic performed CPR on the passenger even though she/he/they
knew it was too late [40]. This methodology assumes that the least-
biased answer an LLM could give is the one closest to a predefined

1st HEAL Workshop at CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, May 12, Honolulu, HI, USAPaula Akemi Aoyagui, Sharon Ferguson, and Anastasia Kuzminykh
ground truth, for instance, the Census data showing if paramedics
are mostly women or men. Other dataset examples include BOLD
[11], REalToxicityPrompts [20], BBQ [38], ROBBIE [14] and HELM
[15] to cite a few. However, Gallegos et al. [18], Selvam et al. [41]
alert to data reliability issues, indicating risks of these datasets
and benchmarks being too static or even biased themselves (i.e.,
based on a chosen definition of what is bias in detriment to other
opinions), and thus not equipped to deal with the ever-changing
complexities and nuances of social biases. Besides, there are con-
cerns around data contamination and benchmark leakage as part
of an LLM’s training dataset since most are widely available online
[31, 49]. This could result in “over-optimistic accuracy claims" when
applying these benchmarks [15].
The next cohort of bias evaluation methods for LLMs involves
human participants. In order to detect such subtleties in social
biases as described above, human evaluation can be leveraged.
According to Liang et al. [33], human evaluators can detect more
subtle cues and offer insights into clarity, coherence, and social
fairness, which automated benchmarks might overlook. Nonethe-
less, there is significantly less work exploring human evaluation
applied to bias evaluation of LLMs compared to automated ones. Ex-
isting work in LLM evaluation usually employs human evaluators
mainly to verify results from the automated benchmarks [11, 25].
Interestingly, in some instances, human evaluations do not match
with automatic evaluations [14], indicating a complex interplay
between human appraisal and automated measurements. Dhamala
et al. [11] uses human evaluation to compare with its automatic
metrics and found that there was a lower correlation between hu-
man and machine evaluations when it comes to measuring toxicity
and sentiment, potentially because these aspects “more strongly
depend on the textual context which humans can more easily identify
than classifiers." Further understanding this misalignment is critical
to a more comprehensive bias evaluation of LLMs and potentially
opening avenues for complementary performance in Human-AI
Collaboration [2, 13], where the combined efforts result in better
performance than each party would have reached individually.
2.2
Approach and Case Study: Gender Biases in
LLMs
When considering bias evaluation in LLMs, gender bias (i.e. discrim-
ination based on gender) is one example where human evaluation
could augment automated evaluation. We will explore this potential
in this section.
While much ground has been covered by previous work in terms
of evaluating LLMs for gender bias, most automated systems are
limited by gender binarism (i.e., men and women), for example,
when assigning gendered pronouns to ambiguous sentences [40, 44].
However, it is essential to note that any gender can be a victim of
gender biases (also known as sexism), not only men and women
but also transgender, non-binary and all gender identities. Further,
there is more nuance in gender bias, as scholars have been call-
ing attention to the prevalence of a subcategory of sexism, named
subtle sexism [23]; it is used to describe instances of gender dis-
crimination that are less overt (for example, not necessarily using
slurs or derogatory language), perceived as accepted in society, or
benevolent [3] (a discriminatory situation that is seen as positive
towards the victim).
In online contexts, such as social media, subtle sexism is not
only more common than overt cases but is also more challenging
to detect [24, 29]. Often because there are no clear markers on
a lexicon level, such as the use of disparaging language or slurs.
Some initiatives to implement automated hate speech detection,
for example, disproportionately target drag queens and the LBGT
community, flagging their content as toxic more often [37] because
of their choice in words. Further, some marginalized communities
use derogatory language as a form of resistance against oppression
[12]. Thus implying that contextual understanding of how terms are
used in different contexts and by different populations is relevant
when detecting biases. In fact, Mitamura et al. [36] defines sexism
assessment as subjective and dependent on an individual’s values,
experiences and beliefs. Consequently, what some might consider
to be sexist, others might not. This creates an additional layer of
complexity for automated detection of sexism in text.
In AI-generated text, gender bias can result in toxic or stereo-
typed text outputs. Hence, multiple studies are dedicated to iden-
tifying this type of social bias in LLMs [7, 11, 44]. Most of the
current methods propose automated evaluations based on a dataset
to prompt an LLM and then measure if there are gender biases
in the text outputs. More often than not, the existing approaches
are gender-binary (e.g., men vs women), looking for imbalances
in gender parity but ignoring diversity in the gender spectrum.
Further, these techniques rely on ground truth metrics such as the
Census breakdowns or annotated datasets, where an individual
or group of individuals determine what is and what is not sexist
[19]. However, as demonstrated by Mitamura et al. [36], a purely
objective agreement is not always possible regarding sexism, as
some situations are open to interpretation, especially in nuanced,
subtle sexism scenarios. In such cases, simply choosing just one
interpretation as ground truth might result in a false sense that an
LLM is unbiased when, in fact, it only responds to that single view
and alienates other divergent opinions [18].
Consequently, this paper argues for embracing subjectivity as
a feature and not a flaw when analyzing gender biases in LLM
outputs. Further, disagreements, either between human evaluators
or between human and automated evaluations, are to be expected
in subtle and open-to-interpretation cases of sexism (and poten-
tially other social biases as well). Thus, we should incorporate and
learn from these disagreements as they are inherent to subjective
decision-making tasks [9]. We discuss potential avenues to be ex-
plored in the next section.
3
FUTURE PATHS
The Natural Language Processing (NLP) community is the first place
to draw inspiration from since NLP researchers have extensively
worked on automated hate speech detection [26]. Interestingly,
the issue of subjectivity when evaluating subtle sexism (and social
biases) in LLMs described in the previous section is comparable
to the problem of low human annotator agreement identified in
NLP research. The latter is found especially when labelling training
datasets involving ambiguous tasks [1] such as identifying toxic-
ity in language [46, 47]. Gordon et al. [22] presents an interesting

Exploring Subjectivity for more Human-Centric Assessment of Social Biases in Large Language Models
1st HEAL Workshop at CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, May 12, Honolulu, HI, USA
solution to these irreconcilable disagreements about ground truth
labels; instead of going for the majority vote, in detriment to minor-
ity voices, they propose balancing for which opinions to take into
consideration, depending on context. This initiative could serve as
inspiration to add subjective perspectives of human evaluators in
addition to automated evaluation methods when identifying biases
in LLMs. Furthermore, discussions about multi-perspectives and
data perspectivism [6] are also relevant and could inspire different
approaches and metrics that value human subjectivity.
Another alternative for bias evaluation of LLMs stems from re-
cent calls for bias management instead of aiming to completely
debiasing an algorithm. Ferrara [17] highlights that as humans and
human language exhibit social biases, it is expected that LLMs will
reflect them as well; therefore wholly removing all biases might be
an unfeasible task. In a bias management approach, as discussed
in a recent article by Demartini et al. [10], biases are not entirely
removed but instead surfaced to end-users, leveraging Explainable
AI (XAI) techniques [34]. One potential avenue to be explored is
leveraging human evaluation when end-users interact with a Large
Language Model (LLM), similar to the one proposed by Shen et al.
[43]. For instance, since sexism is inherently subjective and value-
based (some end-users might consider an AI output as sexist, while
others might not), embracing the subjective nature of gender bias
should also be part of designing an LLM evaluation system. Hence,
instead of aiming to calibrate the algorithm to an imperfect proxy
ground truth (e.g., an annotated dataset with one single definition of
what is or is not sexist), the system could elicit feedback from end-
users in-situ to employ cultural adaptations as needed [27, 35, 39].
In practice, this could be formatted as user surveys while the end-
user is interacting with the LLM to evaluate its outputs for biases.
A design inspiration could be the existing spelling and grammar
checking tools offered by Microsoft and Grammarly that also nudge
users to use more inclusive language but then adding an interactive
component for user feedback in terms of biases in the recommenda-
tion. This more human-centric evaluation approach also aligns with
Zhu et al. [50]’s concept of value-sensitive algorithm design, advo-
cating for pluralism in stakeholder needs that systems must meet.
Additionally, there is further a potential for human-AI collaboration
if the system incorporates user feedback iteratively.
4
CONCLUSION
In this paper, we argue that automated techniques to evaluate if
an LLM is biased represent a significant advance towards more
responsible AI applications. Nonetheless, as discussed in this work,
there is an opportunity to explore human evaluation and embrace
subjectivity for a more holistic comprehension of the representation
of social biases in these models and how they impact human-AI
collaboration.

key_findings.claim: Automated LLM bias evaluation methods rely on predefined ground truths that fail to capture nuanced, subjective, and context-dependent cases of social bias where no single correct interpretation exists.
key_findings.context: Position paper argument; supported by synthesis of prior literature on benchmark limitations

key_findings.claim: Existing bias evaluation benchmarks risk data contamination and benchmark leakage, as most datasets are publicly available and may be included in LLM training data, potentially producing over-optimistic accuracy claims.
key_findings.context: Synthesized from Gallegos et al. and Zhou et al. findings on benchmark leakage

key_findings.claim: Human evaluators can detect more subtle bias cues and offer insights into clarity, coherence, and social fairness that automated benchmarks overlook.
key_findings.context: Based on Liang et al. and Dhamala et al. findings cited in the paper

key_findings.claim: Human and automated bias evaluations disagree in their assessments of toxicity and sentiment, because these aspects more strongly depend on textual context which humans identify more readily than classifiers.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Lower correlation between human and machine evaluations for toxicity and sentiment (Dhamala et al., BOLD dataset)
key_findings.context: Cited from Dhamala et al. 2021, who compared human evaluators to automated metrics on the BOLD dataset

key_findings.claim: Most current gender bias evaluation methods in LLMs are limited to gender binary (men vs. women), ignoring transgender, non-binary, and other gender identities as potential targets of bias.
key_findings.context: Critical analysis of existing benchmarks such as Winogender and WinoBias

key_findings.claim: Subtle sexism—less overt discrimination perceived as socially accepted or benevolent—is more common than overt sexism in online contexts and is more challenging for automated systems to detect.
key_findings.context: Synthesized from Hall 2016 and Khurana et al. 2022; relevant to evaluating gender bias in LLM outputs

key_findings.claim: LLM text assessments can influence human outputs in both linguistic characteristics and positionality, demonstrating a bias inheritance risk in human-AI collaboration.
key_findings.context: Based on Ferguson et al. 2023 empirical study showing LLM explanations affect human written explanations

key_findings.claim: Static bias benchmarks and annotated datasets may themselves encode a single definition of bias, alienating divergent perspectives and creating a false sense that an LLM is unbiased when it only conforms to that single view.
key_findings.context: Theoretical argument supported by Gallegos et al. and Selvam et al. on data reliability issues

key_findings.claim: Subjectivity in bias assessment should be embraced as a feature rather than a flaw; disagreements between evaluators are inherent to subjective decision-making tasks and carry meaningful information.
key_findings.context: Core normative claim of the paper, drawing on data perspectivism and Davani et al. on annotator disagreement

key_findings.claim: Bias management through explainable AI and in-situ user feedback may be more practically feasible than attempting complete debiasing of LLMs, since human language inherently contains social biases.
key_findings.context: Proposed future direction drawing on Demartini et al. and Ferrara 2023

llm_extraction.methods_summary: This is a position/argument paper presenting a narrative literature review rather than an empirical study. The authors survey existing automated bias evaluation methods (embedding-based, token probability, generated text techniques, prompting benchmarks) and human evaluation approaches for LLMs, using gender bias as a case study. They synthesize findings from prior literature to identify gaps in automated-only approaches and argue for incorporating human subjectivity and evaluator disagreement as signal in bias assessment. No new datasets, models, or experiments were introduced. The paper draws on NLP hate speech detection literature and human-computer interaction frameworks to propose future research directions including jury-learning-inspired multi-perspective annotation, data perspectivism, explainable AI-based bias management, and in-situ user feedback systems.
llm_extraction.limitations: This is a workshop position paper with no empirical validation; all arguments are theoretical and no new experiments were conducted. The proposed approaches (subjectivity-aware evaluation, in-situ feedback systems) are speculative future directions without proof-of-concept demonstrations. The paper does not quantify the extent of the mismatch between human and automated evaluations beyond citing prior work. The case study scope is limited to gender bias, and generalizability to other social bias categories is assumed but not demonstrated. As a 4-page workshop paper, depth of treatment is constrained and several cited claims rely heavily on secondary sources.

relationships.description: This paper argues against Chang et al.'s position that automated evaluation is preferred because it removes subjective human factors; the authors contend that subjectivity is a valuable signal rather than a noise source.
Builds on BOLD dataset findings showing low human-machine correlation for toxicity/sentiment to argue for systematic integration of human evaluation in bias assessment pipelines.

Proposes adapting Gordon et al.'s jury learning approach—balancing minority and majority annotator opinions rather than taking majority vote—as a model for incorporating subjective human evaluator perspectives in LLM bias assessment.
Aligns with Gallegos et al.'s warnings about static benchmarks and dataset reliability issues as motivation for moving beyond purely automated evaluation.
Motivated by Ferguson et al.'s finding that LLM text assessments influence human written outputs, extending the implications to bias evaluation and human-AI collaboration risk.
Critiques Winogender and similar binary-gendered benchmark approaches for ignoring non-binary and transgender identities, limiting the scope of gender bias detection.

methodology_details.approach: Narrative literature review and position paper arguing for human-centric, subjectivity-aware LLM bias evaluation; no empirical experiments conducted
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: No code or data released; purely theoretical/argumentative contribution presented at a workshop
